title: Vaccinations for Adults: Why They Matter and Key Ones to Know
content:
Vaccines train the immune system to recognise and fight specific pathogens without causing the disease itself. Vaccination is one of the most cost-effective public health interventions in history, responsible for the eradication of smallpox and the near-elimination of polio worldwide.

Vaccines work by introducing an antigen — a harmless piece of the pathogen (such as a protein from its surface), an inactivated or weakened form of the pathogen, or instructions for the body to make such a protein (as in mRNA vaccines) — to trigger an immune response. The immune system then produces antibodies and memory cells so that future exposure to the real pathogen is neutralised quickly.

Herd immunity occurs when enough people in a community are immune (through vaccination or prior infection) that transmission chains break down, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated (newborns, immunocompromised individuals). Different diseases require different vaccination rates to achieve herd immunity — measles requires about 95 percent coverage.

Key adult vaccines recommended by the CDC (consult your provider for your personalised schedule):

Influenza: Annually, before flu season. Updated each year to match circulating strains.

Td/Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis): Tdap once as an adult if not previously received; then Td booster every 10 years. Pregnant women should receive Tdap in each pregnancy.

COVID-19: Initial series plus updated booster doses as recommended; formulations are updated for new variants.

Shingles (Recombinant Zoster Vaccine, RZV / Shingrix): Two doses for adults 50 and older. Shingles (herpes zoster) causes painful rash and can lead to persistent nerve pain; the vaccine is over 90% effective.

Pneumococcal vaccines: Recommended for adults 65+ and younger adults with certain health conditions (asthma, heart disease, diabetes, smoking) to prevent pneumococcal pneumonia and meningitis.

HPV (Human Papillomavirus): Recommended up to age 26 for all adults who were not vaccinated in adolescence; shared decision-making for ages 27–45.

Vaccines undergo rigorous clinical trials before approval and are continuously monitored for safety after release. Serious adverse events are rare and are carefully tracked through systems such as the US Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). The scientific consensus — supported by thousands of independent studies — is that the benefits of recommended vaccines far outweigh their risks.
